questions.question: Why is speech recognition harder than classifying a whole audio clip into one label?
options: Audio clips never contain silence
The system must output a variable-length token sequence whose timing is not known in advance
Speech recognition only works on stereo audio
Words always align one-to-one with fixed-size frames
questions.explanation: The lesson frames ASR as a structural alignment problem rather than a single-label classification problem. Audio frames and output tokens do not line up one-to-one, and the number of output tokens is unknown before decoding.

questions.question: What does a word-level error metric generally need to account for when comparing a transcript to a reference?
options: Only substitutions
Only insertions
Substitutions, deletions, and insertions
Only timing offsets
questions.explanation: The lesson defines WER using the three standard edit operations from Levenshtein distance. ASR quality is not just about wrong words replacing correct ones, but also about missing or extra words.

questions.question: In greedy CTC decoding, what do you do after taking the per-frame argmax sequence?
options: Reverse the token order and drop vowels
Collapse consecutive repeats and remove blank tokens
Average all token probabilities into one final token
Run a second FFT over the logits
questions.explanation: The lesson's CTC decoder follows two rules: merge repeated consecutive predictions and remove the blank symbol. That is how a long frame-level output collapses into the final transcript string.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of RNN-T over plain CTC emphasized in the lesson?
options: It never needs training labels
It adds token-history conditioning, giving a streamable model with an internal language model
It removes the need for an encoder
It guarantees lower WER than all attention models
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that CTC assumes conditional independence across frames, so it lacks an internal language model. RNN-T adds a predictor over previous tokens plus a joiner, preserving streamability while modeling token history.

questions.question: How does the lesson define Word Error Rate (WER)?
options: (Correct words) / (Predicted words)
(S + D + I) / N using word-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions
(Character edits) / (Audio duration in seconds)
1 - BLEU score
questions.explanation: WER is defined in the lesson as (S + D + I) divided by the number of reference words N. It is the word-level Levenshtein distance normalized by reference length, so lower is better.
